clue.text: A playful nymph might thus be yours

definitions.text: A playful nymph might thus be yours

parts.words: A playful nymph might thus be yours
parts.note: a letter signed off by a faithful sprite would close with the adverb that matches the title of Margaret Kennedy's novel about a devoted nymph

explanation.surface: A frisky water-spirit signs off her love letter.
explanation.walkthrough: Margaret Kennedy's 1924 bestseller was The Constant Nymph; such a nymph would sign her letters 'Yours ...' with the matching adverb, a common letter ending.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means faithfully or unceasingly, the way a devoted correspondent signs off a letter.

clue.text: Is the primate able to produce this delicacy?

parts.note: can means is able
an ape is a primate

explanation.surface: Can a monkey make this party snack?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is the primate able?' is the question 'can ape?', whose two words run together give the snack.
explanation.definitionFit: A small savoury cracker or bread with a topping, served at parties as a delicacy.

clue.text: The altogether the king was in? Throw him out of court! It's non-U !

definitions.text: The altogether the king was in? Throw him out of court! It's non-U !

parts.words: The altogether the king was in? Throw him out of court! It's non-U !
parts.note: the emperor in the fable wore nothing, a lack of clothes; a legal term for dismissing a case; and the letters of the closing phrase rearrange to the same word

explanation.surface: A naked monarch is thrown out of court for vulgarity.
explanation.walkthrough: Three readings: 'the altogether' (nakedness) of Andersen's emperor is no suit; to nonsuit is to dismiss a plaintiff's case; and IT'S NON-U holds the same letters. 'Non-U' is British slang for not upper-class.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal judgment stopping a plaintiff's action, and literally the absence of clothes the fabled emperor paraded in.

clue.text: Where Trelawney did not die, but won the prize

definitions.text: Where Trelawney did not die, but won the prize

parts.words: Where Trelawney did not die, but won the prize
parts.note: Squire Trelawney is a character in Stevenson's pirate novel who survives the voyage and shares the buried hoard

explanation.surface: A Cornish name lived on and took the award.
explanation.walkthrough: Squire Trelawney survives Stevenson's 1883 adventure story and comes home rich with the pirates' gold.
explanation.definitionFit: Stevenson's novel and the isle in it where the squire's party finds Flint's hoard.

clue.text: Is she the craziest Roman of them all?

indicators.note: the maddest arrangement of the word Roman scrambles its letters

explanation.surface: Asking whether one woman is the most deranged of all the Romans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Craziest' turns the letters of ROMAN into a woman's name, also Bellini's druid priestess.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's first name, and the title heroine of Bellini's opera, so a female person.

clue.text: They enjoyed the fruits of unemployment

definitions.text: They enjoyed the fruits of unemployment

parts.words: They enjoyed the fruits of unemployment
parts.note: in the Odyssey a people ate the lotus fruit and lost all wish to work or go home

explanation.surface: Idlers who lived well on the dole.
explanation.walkthrough: Homer's lotus-eaters ate a fruit that made them forget home and duty, so their idleness came from fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek name for Homer's lotus-eaters, who lived in dreamy idleness after eating the lotus.

clue.text: A character on the staff

parts.note: the staff is the musical stave and the character a symbol written at its start to fix the pitch of the lines

explanation.surface: Somebody memorable among the office employees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' suggests a person and 'staff' the employees, but in music the staff is the five-line stave and the character is a written sign.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical sign placed at the start of a stave to fix which note each line stands for.

clue.text: Of the priests that take us to book

indicators.note: take away the word us from the end of the biblical title

parts.note: Leviticus is the third book of the Bible
taken as written

explanation.surface: Priests who lead us to a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take us to book' reads as 'take US from a book': Leviticus without its US leaves the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective refers to the Levites, the Israelite priestly tribe, so it means priestly.

clue.text: Morton's weapon and Uriah's (in common parlance) on a permanent basis

parts.note: Morton's fork was Cardinal Morton's two-pronged tax argument

indicators.note: common speech drops the aspirate, so the initial H goes

parts.note: Uriah Heep is the creeping clerk in Dickens's David Copperfield

explanation.surface: Two historical characters' belongings are kept for good.
explanation.walkthrough: Cardinal Morton's fork was a dilemma for taxpayers; dropping the H in Cockney style turns HEEP'S into 'EEPS.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means for good, with no intention of giving back.

clue.text: The ordinary concern of moneylenders

parts.note: simple means plain or ordinary
interest is concern or involvement

explanation.surface: What ordinarily worries lenders.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue defines the basic charge on a loan; read in parts, ordinary is SIMPLE and concern is INTEREST.
explanation.definitionFit: Interest computed only on the original principal, the plain sort charged by lenders.

clue.text: No Anglican, it seems, for the time being

parts.note: no as a prefix of negation
CE stands for the Church of England, the Anglican church

explanation.surface: Someone is apparently not a member of the established church for now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It seems' is a link: someone not Church of England would be 'non-C of E', and NON plus CE gives the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done for the nonce is done for the present occasion only, a temporary arrangement.

clue.text: He makes a game recovery

parts.note: game here means shot birds, and a gundog fetches them back for the hunter

explanation.surface: A sportsman bravely fights back from illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game recovery' reads as a plucky comeback; in fact game is shot birds, and a breed of gundog is named for fetching them.
explanation.definitionFit: A gundog trained to fetch shot birds back to the hunter.

clue.text: Without its initial piano accompaniment it would abandon the blues for the reds

definitions.text: Without its initial piano accompaniment it would abandon the blues for the reds

parts.words: Without its initial piano accompaniment it would abandon the blues for the reds
parts.note: take the musical piano symbol P off the front of this old German state, famed for a blue pigment, and you get the Soviet land of the communist reds

explanation.surface: A singer drops the blues and turns to red-hot numbers once the pianist leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: Prussian blue is a pigment; remove the initial P (piano, softly, in music) and you have RUSSIA, home of the communist Reds.
explanation.definitionFit: The former German kingdom gave its name to the dye Prussian blue; lose its P and it becomes the Soviet heartland of the Reds.

clue.text: One with expectations that are great, if diminutive, in the laboratory

parts.words: One with expectations that are great
parts.note: Pip is the hero of Dickens's Great Expectations
-ette is a suffix making a small version of something

explanation.surface: A small-scale hopeful at work in the lab.
explanation.walkthrough: 'If' is a link. Pip has great expectations in Dickens; the French diminutive -ette shrinks him.
explanation.definitionFit: A slender glass tube used by chemists for measuring small quantities of liquid, a piece of lab kit.

clue.text: Bad weather portended by the leaves? Or Much Ado About Nothing

definitions.text: Bad weather portended by the leaves?

explanation.surface: Tea-leaf reading forecasts a gale, or a Shakespeare comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense reads the idiom literally: tea leaves read as a fortune foretelling a squall in the cup.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means a great fuss over a trivial matter, and read literally it is a squall inside a china vessel full of tea.

clue.text: One can take time, not heartlessly, wandering about

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
a tin is a can
an era is a period of time

indicators.note: without its heart the word not loses its middle letter, keeping only the first and last

explanation.surface: A tramp takes his time, kindly, as he roams.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take' is a link. 'Heartlessly' strips the middle O from NOT to leave NT.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes someone travelling from place to place, never settled.

clue.text: "Neither a borrower, nor a lender be '" was one of them

definitions.text: "Neither a borrower, nor a lender be '" was one of them

parts.words: "Neither a borrower, nor a lender be '" was one of them
parts.note: Polonius gives his son Laertes a string of maxims in Hamlet, of which this is the best known

explanation.surface: A famous line of advice from Hamlet is quoted.
explanation.walkthrough: Polonius's advice to Laertes in Hamlet is a set of rules for conduct; this line is one of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Rules of conduct or maxims, such as Polonius gives his son.

clue.text: General way of making a takeover

definitions.text: General way of making a takeover

parts.words: General way of making a takeover
parts.note: a general here is an army officer, who commandeers property for military use

explanation.surface: The usual method for a company acquisition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'General' reads as an adjective (usual) but is the military officer, who seizes supplies by official demand.
explanation.definitionFit: Official commandeering of goods or property, especially by the army, is a forcible taking over.

clue.text: Question, answer — a U.S.S.R. problem — baffling astronomers too

indicators.note: the letters pose a problem and are rearranged

parts.note: the Soviet Union's initials, taken as written

explanation.surface: A Soviet riddle that also puzzles stargazers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Problem' rearranges A, A and USSR into UASARS after Q. 'Too' is a link. These objects puzzled astronomers in the 1960s.
explanation.definitionFit: Quasi-stellar radio sources, discovered in the 1960s, whose nature long puzzled astronomers.

clue.text: The requisite cash

explanation.surface: The money required.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The needful' is old British slang for money as well as what is necessary.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means what is necessary, and as colloquial slang it means money.

clue.text: Featured in The Renown before this

indicators.note: the answer appears as a run of letters within the ship's name

explanation.surface: A mention in the warship's records.
explanation.walkthrough: HMS Renown was a famous British battlecruiser, which makes the phrase read as a newspaper item.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic phrase meaning before now, previously.

clue.text: Did he have a good time at the tail-end?

definitions.text: Did he have a good time at the tail-end?

parts.words: Did he have a good time at the tail-end?
parts.note: two set phrases share one first name: a good-time reveller and the tail-end rear gunner of a bomber

explanation.surface: A partygoer asks whether someone enjoyed the end of the evening.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'good-time Charlie' is a pleasure seeker; 'tail-end Charlie' was RAF slang for the rear gunner, so the question asks whether one man was both.
explanation.definitionFit: The first name appears in both 'good-time' and 'tail-end' idioms for a carefree fellow and a rearmost gunner.

clue.text: Not accosted with impunity in the Himalayas

definitions.text: Not accosted with impunity in the Himalayas

parts.words: Not accosted with impunity in the Himalayas
parts.note: a female mountain beast guarding cubs is dangerous to approach

explanation.surface: A climber warns that meeting someone in the mountains is risky.
explanation.walkthrough: The danger is a mother animal of the Himalayan forests, notoriously fierce when protecting young.
explanation.definitionFit: The female of a large, dangerous ursine animal found in the Himalayas.

clue.text: Wheat with silver skin

parts.note: s. stood for the shilling, a silver coin in British money
a pelt is an animal's skin

explanation.surface: Grain with a silvery husk.
explanation.walkthrough: The shilling, written s., was a silver coin in pre-decimal British currency, which is how 'silver' gives S.
explanation.definitionFit: An old variety of hulled grain, a species related to common bread wheat.

clue.text: Hillbilly : changes locale and sex

parts.note: move the hill to flat country and turn the boy's name Billy into a girl's name

explanation.surface: A mountain man moves to town and has a gender change.
explanation.walkthrough: Hill becomes its flat opposite and Billy a female name; the result is a homely woman.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a homely, unglamorous woman: the hill turned to flat country and the boy to a girl.

clue.text: The end, bilingually, of a sprite

parts.note: el is the Spanish for the
fin is the French for end

explanation.surface: A fairy's story ends in two languages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bilingually' says the two pieces come from two languages: Spanish 'el' and French 'fin'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things like a small fairy creature, so it means relating to a sprite.

clue.text: Ornamentally used — for window-dressing?

explanation.surface: Decorations for a shop display.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is the band worn across the body as decoration; the second the sliding frame of a window, which 'dresses' it.
explanation.definitionFit: A decorative band worn over the shoulder, and also the glazed frame of a sash window.

clue.text: Book of Acts?

parts.note: acts here are parliamentary statutes, not the New Testament book

explanation.surface: A reference to the fifth book of the New Testament.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bible's Book of Acts misleads: the acts are Acts of Parliament, and the body of them is written law.
explanation.definitionFit: The body of law laid down by Acts of Parliament, as opposed to common law.
